<reason>A supplied the stronger comparative justification: prioritize meaningful access to experiences digital programs cannot replace, without requiring completed facilities or universal participation. A directly answered the pressure questions and acknowledged that useful digital expansion could be delayed. B established genuine costs for students with ready digital options, but repeatedly exaggerated physical provision’s necessary infrastructure and staffing requirements. Its need-matching alternative was plausible, yet matching remedies to needs did not resolve which receives scarce expansion resources first. A’s closing exposed that unresolved allocation problem more convincingly than B’s claim that its approach could protect everyone without tradeoffs.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A challenged B’s assertion that digital clubs did not compete with playground funding by invoking B’s own finite-budget premise. B then acknowledged that competition but still asserted that delaying digital spending could provide no physical-access benefit. That unsupported leap substantially weakened B’s decisive claim that sequencing imposed costs without gains.</best_rebuttal>
